IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Kozma v. Island Health,

2021 BCSC 687

Date: 20210329

Docket:
S202555

Registry: Victoria

Between:

Justin
Shaundor Kozma

Plaintiff

And

Island
Health

Defendant

The Plaintiff appearing on his own behalf
via teleconference:

J.
Kozma

Counsel for the Defendant via
teleconference:

E.

Vancouver,

[
1
]

THE COURT: This decision was delivered in the
form of Oral Reasons. The Reasons have since been edited for publication.

[
2
]

The defendant, the Vancouver Island Health Authority (referred to in the
initial pleadings as “Island Health”), applies under Rule 9-5 of the
Supreme
Court Civil Rules
[the
Rules
]

for an order striking the
plaintiff’s notice of civil claim (the “NOCC”) on the basis that it discloses
no reasonable claim, is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, or vexatious, and
is otherwise an abuse of the process of this Court.

[
3
]

The plaintiff, Justin Kozma, is self-represented in this litigation.
Based on the evidence before me, it appears that on January 25, 2019, police
brought Mr. Kozma to the Royal Jubilee Hospital in Victoria, BC after he was
observed to be unresponsive lying on the side of the road.

[
4
]

At the Royal Jubilee Hospital the plaintiff was assessed by an emergency
physician who completed a Form 4 Certificate confirming that the plaintiff was being
involuntarily detained pursuant to
s. 22
of the
Mental Health Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 288. The plaintiff was subsequently assessed by another
psychiatrist who completed a similar form. The plaintiff received treatment at
the Royal Jubilee Hospital as a result of those certifications. On February 3,
2019, Mr. Kozma challenged his involuntary detention by seeking a review panel
hearing pursuant to
s. 25
of the
Mental Health Act
. Following a hearing
on February 19, 2019, the review panel determined the plaintiff’s detention
should continue. It does not appear to me that the plaintiff sought judicial
review of the review panel’s decision.

[
5
]

The plaintiff was subsequently discharged from care. On August 6, 2020,
the plaintiff filed his NOCC against the defendant.

Legal framework for a motion to strike a pleading

[
6
]

The defendant relies on R. 9-5(1), particularly grounds (a), (b), and (d).
The rule provides:

9-5(1) At any stage of a proceeding, the court may order to
be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading, petition or other
document on the ground that

(a) it discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as the case
may be,

(b) it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c )it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or
hearing of the proceeding, or

(d) it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may pronounce
judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the
costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
7
]

With respect to applications to strike a pleading on the basis that it does
not disclose a reasonable claim under R. 9-5(1)(a), evidence is not admissible:
R. 9-5(2). Instead, I am to assume “all of the facts alleged will be
established in evidence”:
Kripps v. Touche Ross & Co
. (1992),
1992 CanLII 923 (BC CA)
, 69
B.C.L.R. (2d) 62 at para.
6
, 94 D.L.R. (4th) 284 (C.A.);
Johnston v. Rykon

Construction Management Ltd
.,
2020 BCSC 572
at para.
17
.

[
8
]

On applications to strike under R. 9-5(1)(a), the court can only strike
a claim where the applicant establishes it is “plain and obvious” the pleadings
disclose no reasonable cause of action, the claim has “no reasonable prospect
of success”, or the action is “certain to fail”:
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,

1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 at 980, 49 B.C.L.R. (2d) 273;
R. v. Imperial Tobacco
Canada Ltd.
,
2011 SCC 42
at para.
25
;
International Taoist Church of
Canada v. Ching Chung Taoist Association of Hong Kong Limited
,
2011 BCCA
149
at paras.
20–21
.

[
9
]

A plaintiff is not to be prevented from proceeding with their case
because of the length and complexity of the issues, the novelty of the cause of
action, or the potential for a defendant to present a strong defence:
Hunt

at 980. If there is a chance the plaintiffs might succeed, they are not to be
“driven from the judgment seat”:
Hunt
at 980.

[
10
]

On
a motion to strike pleadings as disclosing no cause of action, I am to read the
pleadings as they are or as they could be amended “as generously as possible
and to accommodate any inadequacies in the form of the allegations which are
merely the result of drafting deficiencies”:
Operation Dismantle v. The
Queen
,
1985 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 441 at 451, 18 D.L.R. (4th) 481, cited with approval
by Frankel J.A. for the court in
Chang Estate v. Chang
,
2010 BCCA 111
at
para.
40
.

[
11
]

With
respect to applications to strike on the basis that a pleading is unnecessary,
scandalous,
frivolous, or vexatious
pursuant to R. 9-5(1)(b), i
n
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish
Congress

(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
,
36 C.P.C. (4th) 266
,
23 B.C.T.C. 98
(Chambers)
, Justice Romilly described what is involved in
the following terms:

[47] … An
“embarrassing” and “scandalous” pleading is one that is so irrelevant that it
will involve the parties in useless expense and will prejudice the trial of the
action by involving them in a dispute apart from the issues:
Keddie v. Dumas
Hotels Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 at 147 (B.C.C.A.). . . . A pleading is
“unnecessary” or “vexatious” if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff’s
cause of action or does not advance any claim known in law:
Strauts v.
Harrigan
,
1992 CanLII 595 (BC SC)
, [1992] B.C.J. No. 86 (Q.L.) (B.C.S.C.)

[
12
]

Such a pleading has also been described as one
that is “hopelessly oppressive” or causes the other party anxiety, trouble, or
expense:
Borsato v. Basra
,
2000 BCSC 28
at
para.
25
(Master), rev’d on other grounds
2000 BCSC 1898
.

[
13
]

With respect to striking a claim on the basis that it is an abuse of
process of the courtpursuant to R. 9-5(1)(d), the defendant argues the
plaintiff’s claim is a collateral attack on the order of his detention and
relies on the following cases for that proposition:
Garland v. Consumers’
Gas Co.
,
2004 SCC 25
at para.
71
;
Toronto

(City) v. C.U.P.E.,
Local 79,

2003 SCC 63
at paras.
23
, 33. A collateral attack involves a
party attempting to challenge the validity of a binding order in the incorrect
forum, rather than using the appropriate direct attack procedure:
Garland

at
para.
71
.

Analysis

[
14
]

The
defendant argues the NOCC is largely unintelligible, confusing, and difficult
to understand, which in itself provides a basis to strike it, relying on
Johnson
v. Smith
,
2018 BCSC 836
at paras.
11–15
. The defendant submits that all it can
discern is a human rights complaint (Part 1, para. 2 of the NOCC), an
allegation of defamation which it says is un-particularized (Part 1, para. 3 of
the NOCC), and a claim for intentional infliction of emotional distress (Part 2,
para. 1a of the NOCC).

[
15
]

I
agree that insofar as the plaintiff seeks to claim for a violation of his human
rights under the
Human Rights Code
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 10
, those must be
pursued by him in accordance with the process set out in the
Human Rights Code
.
However, I do not read Part 1, para. 2 of the NOCC as being limited to such an
allegation. That paragraph also includes references to torture and other
actions aimed at maintaining the plaintiff’s imprisonment.

[
16
]

With
respect to the allegation of defamation, I again agree that the claim does not
particularize the statements the plaintiff alleges were made, or how or when
they were communicated to another party, but defamation is a known and
established cause of action. What is missing are the particulars of the
allegation of the cause of action being claimed. With proper amendments, the
deficiency in this aspect of the plaintiff’s NOCC could be remediated. I am not
prepared to strike that aspect of the plaintiff’s claim. The plaintiff would be
well-advised to review the proper form for such a pleading available from such
texts as John A. Campion et al., eds,
Bullen & Leake & Jacob’s Canadian
Precedents of Pleadings
, 3rd ed. (Toronto: Carswell, 2017).

[
17
]

With
respect to the defendant’s submission that the NOCC is in essence a complaint
about being involuntarily certified, and as such is a collateral attack on the findings
of the review panel, I disagree with that characterization for two reasons.
First, although the NOCC is difficult to understand, I do see that it contains
allegations of fact which implicate the following causes of action: the tort of
false imprisonment, the torts of assault and battery, violations of the
plaintiff’s rights under the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

[
Charter
]
,

and a breach of fiduciary duty.

1.

The tort of
false imprisonment

[
18
]

To
make out the tort of false imprisonment a plaintiff must establish three elements:
(a) they have been totally deprived of their liberty; (b) the deprivation must
have been against their will; and (c) it must have been caused by the
defendant. If a plaintiff establishes those elements, the onus shifts to the
defendant to justify the detention based on legal authority under common law or
statute:
Kovacs v. Ontario Jockey Club
,
1995 CanLII 7397 (ON CTGD)
, 126 D.L.R. (4th) 576 at 585,
[1995] O.J. No. 2181 (Gen. Div.), citing
Kendall v. Gambles Canada Ltd.,

1981 CanLII 2149 (SK QB)
, [1981] 4 W.W.R. 718 at 728, 11 Sask. R. 361 (Q.B.).
Kovacs
has recently
been cited with approval by this Court in
Qiao v. Owners, Strata Plan LMS
3863,
2020 BCSC 818
at para.
116
.

[
19
]

Facts
and other allegations which also seem to involve false or misleading actions
aimed at causing or contributing to the plaintiff’s detention and extension of
that detention appear at Part 1, paras. 2, 7, 12, 18 and 21 of the NOCC.

2.

The torts of battery
and assault

[
20
]

I
also see allegations which implicate the torts of battery and assault.

[
21
]

Battery
involves the intentional infliction of unlawful force on another person:
Norberg
v. Wynrib
,
1992 CanLII 65 (SCC)
, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 226 at 246, 92 D.L.R. (4th) 449.

[
22
]

Mr. Justice Verhoeven wrote at para. 67 of
Kearns v. Marples
,
2009 BCSC 802
:

[67]      Assault is the intentional creation of the
apprehension

of imminent harmful or offensive contact. Battery consists of intentionally
causing a harmful or offensive contact with another person. Assault should be
distinguished from battery, although the two are often blurred together and
called “assault”: Allen M. Linden and Bruce Feldthusen,
Canadian Tort Law
,
8th ed. (LexisNexis Butterworths, 2006) at 46.

[Emphasis added]

[
23
]

Facts
that could constitute allegations of assault & battery are set out at Part
1, paras. 2, 8, 11, 23 and 27 of the NOCC.

3. Violations of Rights under the
Charter

[
24
]

The
plaintiff also alleges violations of numerous rights which he enjoys under the
Charter
,
including freedom of thought, conscience, and expression. To that extent,
please see Part 1, paras. 1, 2a, and 14 of the NOCC.

[
25
]

He
alleges a violation of security of the person (Part 1, para. 2b of the NOCC), as
well as cruel and unusual treatment (Part 1, para. 8 of the NOCC), and a violation
of his right to
habeas corpus
, via being disciplined on attempting to
seek assistance of legal counsel to pursue such relief (Part 1, para. 2c of the
NOCC).

[
26
]

I
pause here to note that I do not read the plaintiff’s NOCC as simply alleging
that the defendant had an obligation to pursue
habeas corpus
on his
behalf. I interpret the claim as being capable of being read and understood as
making a claim that the defendant violated that fundamental freedom of the
plaintiff by in some way restricting his ability to pursue
habeas corpus
.

4. Breach of fiduciary duty

[
27
]

Inferentially,
it appears that the plaintiff is alleging that the Health Authority is in a
special relationship with him, and owes him a fiduciary duty which takes the
form of certain obligations, and that it breached that duty by taking certain
action.

[
28
]

I
note that at Part 1, para. 15 of the NOCC, the plaintiff refers to a breach of
trust.

[
29
]

I
do not say that these claims are well pleaded or that they are sufficiently
particularized, but I simply say that it is not plain and obvious to me that
these claims are bound to fail. It appears to me that they have not yet been
fully particularized, but that they could, with the appropriate amendments, set
out the full factual and legal basis for causes of action that are well-known
and established in law.

[
30
]

I
turn to the second reason why I say that the characterization of the defendant
of the NOCC as a collateral attack is inappropriate. As I understand the NOCC, it
is not limited to the fact that the plaintiff was detained under the
Mental
Health Act
, but rather the NOCC alleges that the detention was a violation
of certain civil and constitutional rights the plaintiff enjoys, which caused
him to suffer damage.

[
31
]

I disagree with the defendant’s submissions that this is a collateral
attack on the review board’s decision to confirm the plaintiff’s detention. It
seems to me that this case is more in line with the circumstances that were
before the Court in
Canada (Attorney General) v. TeleZone Inc.
,
2010 SCC
62
at para.
64
:

[64]

Secondly,
TeleZone is not seeking to “avoid the consequences of [the ministerial]
order issued against it” (
Garland
, at para.
72
). On the
contrary, the ministerial order and the financial losses allegedly consequent
on that order constitute the foundation of the damages claim. This was the
result in
Garland
itself, where Iacobucci J. held for the
Court:

Based on a plain reading of this rule, the
doctrine of collateral attack does not apply in this case because
here
the specific object of the appellant’s action is not to invalidate or render
inoperative the Board’s orders
, but rather to recover money that was
illegally collected by the respondent as a result of Board
orders. Consequently, the collateral attack doctrine does not
apply. [Emphasis added; para. 71.]

[
32
]

Similarly
in this case, as I understand it, the plaintiff is not seeking judicial review
of the review board’s determination. He is seeking a determination that his
detention was unlawful, and that he suffered certain damages as a result of that
detention and his treatment while in the care of the defendant, all of which
breached his civil and constitutional rights.

[
33
]

I
agree the NOCC is poorly drafted. Perhaps, even, very poorly drafted. However,
I am mindful that the plaintiff is self-represented, and I am also mindful that
the plaintiff’s NOCC alleges wrongdoing against him when he was in a highly
vulnerable state. I do not know the current state of the plaintiff’s health,
but I am prepared to give the plaintiff the opportunity to amend the NOCC to
include sufficient particularization of the facts and legal basis to set out
clearly the causes of action he seeks to pursue. In my mind, given the
particular circumstances of this case, and the background of the plaintiff as
set out in the evidence before me, which includes that he is someone with a
history of vulnerability due to mental health issues, this is the more just and
equitable outcome. Therefore, I am exercising my discretion not to strike the
NOCC in this application.

[
34
]

Instead,
I will order that the plaintiff has 60 days to file an amended NOCC.

[
35
]

This
order is without prejudice to the defendant’s right to renew the application to
strike on the ground that the amended pleading still does not disclose a cause
of action, is frivolous, vexatious, or that it is a collateral attack. If an
amended Notice of Civil Claim is not filed within 60 days, this order will stand
as dismissing the claim without the need for a future court application. An
order to that effect may be obtained simply on proof that no amended Notice of Civil
Claim has been filed by the plaintiff within 60 days of this judgment.

[
36
]

I
make no order as to costs.

[
37
]

THE
COURT:
Any questions arising from my reasons?

[
38
]

MR.
VAUGHN:
My Lady, if we may, I would submit that Mr. Kozma’s signature be
dispensed with on the order, but that we provide him with a copy of the draft
order prior to filing if your Ladyship agrees.

[
39
]

THE
COURT:
On what basis do you make that request?

[
40
]

MR.

VAUGHN:
Mr. Kozma is self-represented. It would be more efficient, but
I’m in your hands My Lady.

[
41
]

THE
COURT:
I’m loathe to dispense with Mr. Kozma’s approval of the form of the
order because my order includes conditions for the dismissal of the NOCC.

[
42
]

MR.

VAUGHN:
Alright.

[
43
]

THE
COURT:
If for whatever reason it proves difficult to obtain Mr. Kozma’s
endorsement of the form of the order then you can seek to dispense with his
signature later, but I’m not going to dispense with that now.

[
44
]

MR.

VAUGHN:
Okay.

[
45
]

THE
COURT:
Thank you very much gentleman.

[
46
]

MR.

VAUGHN:
Thank you.

[
47
]

MR.

STANGER:
Thank you.

[
48
]

MR.

KOZMA:
Thank you.

“Jackson
J.”
